supplied for SOLAS size life rafts are appropriate for life rafts of below SOLAS 
size.  
10.2.7 In cases where smaller than SOLAS size life rafts are fitted, and there is any doubt 
with respect to the compatibility of HRU and the raft itself, then confirmation is to 
be sought from manufacturers and/or equipment suppliers that the breaking 
strength of the weak link and the size of the raft are compatible.  
10.2.8 Hammar have also produced a small green cartridge type weak link which is for 
attaching to the standard Hammar HRU. They are now recommending that the 
new green coloured HRU should be used for small rafts.

served by demonstration on board. 
10.4 TYPE APPROVAL 
10.4.1 The surveyor should ensure that all LSA equipment is type approved (MED) where 
required. This should be verified at initial surveys. Equipment that is MED 
approved should follow the requirements of The Merchant Shipping (Marine 
Equipment) Regulations 1999 and MSN 1734 (M+F) - Type Approval of Marine 
Equipment (EC Notified Bodies). 
1.0.4.2 At flag ins the flagging in surveyor is to complete a list of non-MED equipment and 
verify that this equipment is type approved against the relevant standard. The list 
of non-MED equipment is to be attached to the file and the Fishing Vessel

of non-MED equipment is to be attached to the file and the Fishing Vessel

10.4.3 Any non-MED equipment which has been replaced must be replaced with MED 
type approved equipment. 
10.4.4 At annual renewal surveys changes to the equipment list is to be updated.

10.8 EXEMPTIONS/EXCEPTIONS – RESCUE BOATS 
10.8.1 Requirements are contained in MSN 1873, Chapter 7, section 7.2.1.4. 
10.8.2 There are some over 24m metre vessels which have exemptions from the carriage 
of rescue boats. 
10.8.3 Life-Saving Appliances and Arrangements for vessels of 45 m in length and over 
are determined as per Torremolinos Convention and exemption granted be shall 
communicated to the International Maritime Organization(IMO) to the extent 
necessary to confirm that the level of safety is adequately maintained and the IMO 
shall circulate such particulars to the Parties for their information. Therefore, the 
policy is not to grant exemption to this size of vessel. 
10.8.4 Life-Saving Appliances and Arrangements for vessels 24 m to 45 m in len
---CHUNK---

policy is not to grant exemption to this size of vessel. 
10.8.4 Life-Saving Appliances and Arrangements for vessels 24 m to 45 m in length are  
determined by COUNCIL DIRECTIVE 97/70/EC of 11 December 1997 setting up a 
harmonised safety regime for fishing vessels of 24 metres in length and over (the 
EU Directive). 
18.8.5 The EU Directive requires that all vessels over 24 m but less than 45 metres in 
length shall be provided with a rescue boat, “except where the administration is 
satisfied that because of the size and the manoeuvrability of the vessel, the near 
availability of search and rescue facilities and meteorological warning systems, the 
operation of the vessel in areas not susceptible to heavy weather or the seasonal 
characteristics of the operation, such provision is unnecessary.” The EU 
requirement is repeated in MSN 1873 Chapter 7.2.1.4(ii).

considered valid as the regulations are no longer in force and the conditions of the 
exemption are not in line with the current requirements. The exemption is to be 
reviewed in line with the requirements contained in MSN 1873.

proposed as an equivalence for twin rig fishing vessels 24m to 45m only: 
1. The vessel shall be provided with good manoeuvrability and it is likely that 
bow and stern thrusters on larger vessels will be required together with port 
and starboard bridge wing controls so that recovery of the helpless person 
can be observed from the navigating bridge. 
2. The vessel shall be provided with a rescue basket fitted with retro reflective 
tape visible from the sides and above and be provided with powered 
recovery arrangements. The powered recovery arrangements need not be 
dedicated to the rescue basket. 
3. Personnel nominated to assist with the recovery of the casualty into the 
rescue basket shall wear immersion suits and have safety harnesses.

10.9 LIFEJACKETS 
10.9.1 GENERAL 
10.9.1.1 Requirements are contained in MSN 1871, Chapter 7; in MSN 1872, Chapter 7; 
and in MSN 1873, Chapter 7. 
10.9.1.2 No lifejacket should be passed as part of the statutory equipment of a ship unless 
it:- 
• is of an accepted type; 
• complies in all respects with the accepted specification; 
• is in good condition and fit for the service intended. On board repairs or 
modifications are not acceptable. 
10.9.1.3 Any lifejacket supplied new should be MED approved with required wheelmark 
and Type approval certification. 
10.9.1.4 They can be solid-filled type or comply with BS EN 396 or BSEN 399, which will 
eventually be replaced by EN ISO 12402, with automatic gas inflation and at least 
150 Newtons of buoyancy. It should be fitted with retro-reflective tape, a type 
approved light and a whistle. 
10.9.1.4 Lifejackets for seagoing ships in accordance with ISO 12402-1 are intended 
primarily for use on seagoing ships under IMO rul
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
ith retro-reflective tape, a type 
approved light and a whistle. 
10.9.1.4 Lifejackets for seagoing ships in accordance with ISO 12402-1 are intended 
primarily for use on seagoing ships under IMO rules.  
10.9.1.5 PFD, performance level 275, in accordance with ISO 12402-2 are intended 
primarily for offshore use and by people of significant weight or who are using 
items of significant weight and thus require additional buoyancy. They are also of 
value to those who are using clothing which traps air and which will adversely 
affect the self-righting capacity of the lifejacket. They are designed to ensure that 
the user is floating with their mouth and nose clear of the surface at an angle and 
with sufficient freeboard to limit mouth immersions in waves.  
Note: when fitted with emergency light and whistle can be counted as abandon 
ship lifejacket required by MSN1871 Amendment No.2 The Code of Practice for 
the Safety of Small Fishing Vessels of less than 15m Length Overall, or any
---CHUNK---

y light and whistle can be counted as abandon 
ship lifejacket required by MSN1871 Amendment No.2 The Code of Practice for 
the Safety of Small Fishing Vessels of less than 15m Length Overall, or any 
superseding document.  
10.9.1.6 PFD, performance level 150, in accordance with ISO 12402-3 are intended for 
general offshore and rough weather use where a high standard of performance is 
required. As tested, they will turn an unconscious person in swimming attire into a 
safe position. Additionally, they should maintain a fully clothed person in a safe 
position with no subsequent action by the user.

10.10.2 LIFEBUOY SELF-IGNITING LIGHTS 
10.10.2.1 Lights of this type must be self-igniting in water, and be capable of burning brightly 
for at least 2 hours. The lights should be stowed to prevent accidental or 
premature ignition. They may be operated by water activated cells or dry batteries.

possible to prevent inclination of the signal in a seaway.

10.14.2 POWER SUPPLY 
10.14.2.1 The source of energy should have a capacity to ensure at least 8 hour, preferably 
24 hour operation at the highest rated power of the equipment with a duty cycle of 
1:9. This duty cycle is defined as 6 seconds transmission, 6 seconds reception 
above squelch opening level and 48 seconds below squelch opening level. The 
source of energy should comply with the following: 
• A sealed primary battery which should be: 
• of a type which will not emit substances which may be injurious to personnel, 
or damaging to the equipment or fabric of the survival craft. This requirement 
should be met whether the power source is in a stored condition or normal 
use; 
• securely mounted and clearly marked with
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
damaging to the equipment or fabric of the survival craft. This requirement 
should be met whether the power source is in a stored condition or normal 
use; 
• securely mounted and clearly marked with the shelf life whose expiry should 
not be less than 2 years from the date of survey; and 
• the battery should have sufficient capacity so that routine testing of 2 minutes 
once per week should not reduce its capacity below that needed to conform 
to the operational requirements recommended above. Where the battery is 
used to supply power to any other equipment, sufficient capacity should be 
available to operate this equipment at its maximum rated power for the 
period recommended in addition to the radio apparatus. 
10.14.2.2 Batteries should be disposed of strictly in accordance with manufacturer’s 
instructions.

Clear instructions on how to use the fittings in an emergency should be marked on 
the radar transponder or provided in a suitable format for carrying on to the 
survival craft. It is acceptable to mount the equipment within the liferaft, e.g. 
‘hang’, the equipment will operate satisfactorily. Alternatively, the radar

should be include

10.16.6 PERSONAL LOCATOR BEACONS 
10.16.6.1 On vessels of less than 15m, if an EPIRB is carried, then Personal Locator 
Beacons can be either 406 MHz and comply with EN 302 152 or be AIS. If no 
EPIRB is carried, then PLBs must be 406MHz and comply with EN 302 152. This 
is because the EPIRB is considered to be the mandatory equipment and the PLB 
is a voluntary addition. Furthermore, on crewed vessels, some skippers may 
prefer AIS PLBs because this will allow them to locate crew in the water. 
10.16.6.2 On single handed vessels, PLBs shall be 406 MHz PLBs as the AIS is unlikely to 
notify the Coastguard of Man Overboard. 
10.16.6.3 All 406 MHz PLBs must be registered in accordance with The Merchant Shipping 
(EPIRB Registration
---CHUNK---

notify the Coastguard of Man Overboard. 
10.16.6.3 All 406 MHz PLBs must be registered in accordance with The Merchant Shipping 
(EPIRB Registration) Regulations SI 2000, No. 1850 and Merchant Shipping 
Notice 1816 (M&F) – Mandatory Registration of Electronic Position indicating 
Instructions to Surveyors – Life Saving Appliances  Chapter 10

as 0.71. For other materials suitable A values would be considered based on 
metallurgist’s report on any tests. 
10.26.4 FUEL TANKS ETC. 
10.26.4.1 Fuel tanks must be of sufficient capacity for 24 hours continuous operation at 
speed of 6 knots, and should be substantially constructed of steel or other 
accepted material and should be free standing as opposed to built-in design.

copper pipes or fittings, unless adequate precautions are taken against electrolytic 
action. The exterior of the tanks should be protected against corrosion from sea

10.26.5 PROTECTION OF INSTALLATION 
10.26.5.1 The engine and its accessories including the fuel tanks, pipes, and fittings should 
be adequately protected to ensure reliable operation under adverse weather 
conditions with water spraying over the boat and collecting in the bilges. Attention 
should be given to the location of alternators fitted to recharge batteries to ensure 
ease of access and protection from adverse weather or water thrown up by the 
engine flywheel.

10.35 SERVICING OF LSA 
10.35.1 Rigid inflated rescue boats which form part of the ships' Life-Saving Appliances 
are normally required to be serviced annually, and every effort should be made to 
ensure that this is carried out. When, however, it is clearly impracticable to comply 
with this requirement, the servicing may be deferred for a period not exceeding 5 
months. 
10.35.2 At every bi-annual servicing of a rigid inflated rescue boat a 10% overload static 
load test should be carried out with the rescue boat suspended from its lifting hook 
or bridle in accordance with the manufacturer's approved servicing instructions.

10.36 ON BOARD TRAINING AND INSTRUCTIONS 
10.36.1 On-board training in the use of the vessel's life-saving appliances, including 
survival craft equipment, must be given as soon as possible but not later than two 
weeks after a crewmember joins the vessel. However, if the crew member is on a 
regularly scheduled rotating assignment to the vessel, such training must be given 
not later than two weeks after the time of first joining the vessel; 
10.36.2 Instructions in the use of the vessel's life saving appliances and in survival at sea 
shall be given at the same intervals as the drills. Individual instruction may cover 
different parts of the vessel's life-saving system, but all the vess
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
ife saving appliances and in survival at sea 
shall be given at the same intervals as the drills. Individual instruction may cover 
different parts of the vessel's life-saving system, but all the vessel's life-saving 
equipment and appliances shall be covered within any period of two months. Each 
member of the crew should be given instructions which shall include but not 
necessarily be limited to: 
• Operation and use of the vessel's inflatable liferafts, including precautions 
concerning sharp objects; 
• Problems of hypothermia, cold water shock, first-aid treatment for 
hypothermia and other appropriate first aid procedures; 
• Special instructions necessary for use of the vessel's life-saving appliances 
in severe weather and severe sea conditions. 
10.36.3 On-board training in the use of davit-launched liferafts must take place at intervals 
of not more than four months on every vessel fitted with such appliances. 
Whenever practicable this shall include the inflation and loweri
---CHUNK---

of not more than four months on every vessel fitted with such appliances. 
Whenever practicable this shall include the inflation and lowering of a liferaft. This 
liferaft may be a special liferaft intended for training purposes only, which is not 
part of the vessel's life-saving equipment; such a special liferaft shall be 
conspicuously marked.

10.38.2.2 BUILT-IN BUOYANCY AIR CASES 
10.38.2.2.1 Where lifeboats are fitted with built-in buoyancy compartments the surveyor 
should, after careful examination, carry out such tests, which may include tests by 
air pressure, as he considers necessary. A pressure of 10 kgf/m2 is sufficient for 
th
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
y compartments the surveyor 
should, after careful examination, carry out such tests, which may include tests by 
air pressure, as he considers necessary. A pressure of 10 kgf/m2 is sufficient for 
this purpose and should not be exceeded. In order to avoid overstressing the 
compartments, it is strongly recommended that the pressure should be applied by 
means of a hand pump in conjunction with a suitable calibrated mercurial U-tube 
for enabling small differences in pressure to be read. Leakage where indicated, 
may be located by the application of soapy water to the seams. 
10.38.2.3 SOLID BUOYANCY 
10.38.2.3.1 Where solid buoyancy is fitted it will normally be unnecessary, to remove this for 
inspection at each survey unless the surveyor has reason, because of the 
condition or general appearance of the boat, to suspect defects. It should be noted 
that some of the earlier types of solid buoyancy, e.g. polystyrene, were not fully oil 
resistant and were subject to damage from oil le
---CHUNK---

that some of the earlier types of solid buoyancy, e.g. polystyrene, were not fully oil 
resistant and were subject to damage from oil leakage in motor propelled lifeboats. 
Partial opening up should be required to facilitate examination of such material 
and any defective portions should be replaced by an accepted oil resistant 
material which is not chemically incompatible with existing material. 
10.38.2.4 LIFTING HOOKS 
10.38.2.4.1 Careful attention should be paid to the condition of lifting hooks and their 
connection in all lifeboats. Where signs of corrosion are evident in the lifeboat 
lifting connections the lifting hooks should be removed and one or more lifting 
hook connection bolts through keel backed out for examination. Where 
disengaging gear is fitted surveyors should carry out and witness tests in 
accordance recognised procedures.

10.38.2.5 STEEL LIFEBOATS 
10.38.2.5.1 Rust and scale should be removed from steel lifeboats before any detailed 
inspection is carried out. 
10.38.2.6 ALUMINIUM ALLOY LIFEBOATS 
10.38.2.6.1 Aluminium alloy lifeboats should be carefully examined for condition, particularly 
behind the skates, their securing wires and also gripe wires where metals other 
than aluminium may have been in contact with the hull of the lifeboat. Surveyors 
should pay special attention to the riveting of aluminium alloy as in some cases 
rivets of NR6 material were used which have proved to be unsatisfactory. Where 
re-riveting is found to be necessary only rivets of NR5 material should be used.

10.38.2.7 GLASS-REINFORCED PLASTIC LIFEBOATS 
10.38.2.7.1 Glass-reinforced plastic lifeboats should be carefully examined for fractures 
particularly in garboard attachments of built-in buoyancy and the junction of 
thwarts and side seats. Fractures may also have occurred in the horizontal and 
vertical surfaces of side buoyancy and in the gunwale, usually at positions 
approximately one-quarter of the length of the lifeboat from the bow or stern.

10.38.3.2 MOTOR LIFEBOATS AND RESCUE BOATS 
10.38.3.2.1 The machinery of motor lifeboats and rescue boats should be inspected. Engine 
running and manoeuvring trials should be carried out at each survey. The engine 
need only be dismantled for examination if the surveyor has reason to doubt its 
condition and performance. The survey should include the fuel tanks, their filling 
and relief arrangements, the fire extinguishing appliances and, where fitted, the 
searchlight, the radio battery, etc.

---CHUNK---

OTALLY ENCLOSED LIFEBOATS 
10.38.3.4.1 In addition to thither tests required for totally enclosed lifeboats, when a totally 
enclosed lifeboat is in the water the opportunity should be taken to run the engine 
to full operating temperature to see if fumes develop from the exhaust system. 
Surveyors should check that: 
• there are no exhaust system leaks; 
• there are no oil or diesel leaks and the engines are clean; 
• the exhaust and its lagging runs clear of the bilge water area and that there 
is little risk of bilge water contacting the engine manifold and exhausts when 
the boat is in use; 
• exhaust lagging is clean and dry and is provided with suitable protection; 
• bilges are kept dry and clear of oil; and 
• any paint used on engines, manifolds and exhausts does not give off fumes 
when it is heated.

years.

work boat the winches should be opened up for thorough

10.38.6.6.3 There have been reports of some hand brake failures during tests of this type of 
winch. The winch is used normally in conjunction with a single arm davit for 
handling rescue boats. The winch was originally type approved by the MCA in 
1979 for a maximum load of 500 kg and the design is such that an externally fitted 
spring tension holds the hand brake in effective position. The failures reported are 
for winches which have been more recently manufactured and accepted for loads 
higher than 800 kg. 
10.38.6.6.4 Investigations of failure suggest that the spring tension is reduced over time until 
the hand brake is no longer able to hold a heavy load. In each case the 
replacement of the spring rectified the fault. The M
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
ons of failure suggest that the spring tension is reduced over time until 
the hand brake is no longer able to hold a heavy load. In each case the 
replacement of the spring rectified the fault. The MCA has therefore informed the 
manufacturer that such a design of winch will no longer be accepted for UK 
Registered Vessels for a working load over 500 kg. 
10.38.6.6.5 For vessels which already have these winches fitted for loads higher than 500 kg

• sufficient spare springs are carried on the vessel to replace any faulty or 
suspected spring. 
10.38.6.6.6 Although no adverse reports have been received for the winches where the 
working load is 500 kg or less, the winch operators are nevertheless advised to 
inspect the external spring regularly and carry spares.

and Seamen of merchant ships, and Owners, Skippe
---CHUNK---

he MCA considers that the proper number of men for a launching or recovery

fishing vessels are, therefore, asked to note that this number should never be 
exceeded. 
10.38.8.1.3 A notice should be attached to each relevant set of davits or other device stating, 
“Lower or recover with two man crew only”. 
10.38.8.1.4 In the case of a launch/recovery device for an inflatable boat, although in certain 
circumstances the boat is not required to be fitted with an engine, an allowance is 
made in all cases for the weight of an engine and its fuel of at least 60 kgs in case 
one is fitted at a later date. 
Note: Lifeboat Davits must be of sufficient strength to launch the boat and full 
complement. Rescue boat davits must be of sufficient strength to safely enable 
recovery of the rescue boat, it’s equipment and full complement of persons.

and lifeboatmen.

10.39.7 INSTALLATION AND INSPECTION OF DISENGAGING GEARS 
10.39.7.1 In dealing with the installation of disengaging gears surveyors should satisfy 
themselves that such gears comply in all respects with the specification referred to 
in the certificate. Fitting should be carried out strictly in accordance with the 
accepted arrangements and the gear should be subjected to the programme of 
tests detailed in MSN 1803. 
10.39.8 TESTS AT PERIODIC SURVEYS 
10.39.8.1 At the periodic surveys of MCA on board ships, disengaging gears should be 
tested to ensure the simultaneous release when the lifeboat or rescue boats are 
waterborne. Where the rods are found to be defective in certain standard type 
disengaging gear

gaging gears should be

waterborne. Where the rods are found to be defective in certain standard type 
disengaging gear comprising part rod, part chain release, they should be replaced 
with all chain release. When the surveyor is satisfied that the simultaneous release 
mechanism is in good working order it should be further tested with the lifeboat 
suspended just above the water to ensure that release does not take place until

10.39.9 STATUTORY PROOF TESTING OF DISENGAGING GEARS 
10.39.9.1 The Merchant Shipping (Life-Saving Appliances for Ships other than Ships of 
Classes III to VI(A)) Regulations 1999 require (among other things) that “at least 
once every 5 years rescue boats and lifeboats shall be turned out and lowered 
when loaded with weights to simulate 1.1 times the total mass of the lifeboat or 
rescue boat when loaded with its full complement of persons and equipment and 
whenever the release gear is overhauled”. 
10.39.9.2 Such a test is intended to prove the adequacy of every part of the fully loaded 
launching system such as davits, winches and their foundations; falls, blocks, 
connecting loose gear such as shackles, rings; release gear hooks and their 
connections to the boat etc. In addition,
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
launching system such as davits, winches and their foundations; falls, blocks, 
connecting loose gear such as shackles, rings; release gear hooks and their 
connections to the boat etc. In addition, it tests the tricing and bowsing 
arrangements and load distribution on the boat itself as would be imposed in a 
real evacuation situation. 
10.39.9.3 Some shipowners have approached the MCA for guidance in conducting this test 
safely. The MCA has therefore consulted the relevant experts in the field and one 
method of carrying out the test safely is described in this paragraph.

10.39.9.4 The shipowner must look ahead and plan such tests. The launching device 
comprises many specialised components which require regular inspection, 
maintenance, replacement, overhaul etc. by specially trained personnel which 
should best be completed before the test. There may be a large number of
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
ed components which require regular inspection, 
maintenance, replacement, overhaul etc. by specially trained personnel which 
should best be completed before the test. There may be a large number of boats 
to test (e.g. for large passenger ships), so a regular programme of tests spread 
over five years to cover all the boats may be essential. 
10.39.9.5 Having decided to test a particular boat, preliminary inspection of key parts likely 
to be stressed during the test needs to be made. If specialised help from 
manufacturers is not available, the ship’s Chief Engineer (or his delegate) should 
carry out such an inspection following the manufacturer’s manuals and general 
engineering principles. In addition, ship’s LSA maintenance logs are to be 
scrutinised to confirm evidence of regular maintenance and history of any 
persistent problem or major fault. 
10.39.9.6 It is also necessary to carry out an audit of certificates on board for falls, blocks, 
loose gear, davits, winches, relea
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MSIS27.10_R9.21.pdf
maintenance and history of any 
persistent problem or major fault. 
10.39.9.6 It is also necessary to carry out an audit of certificates on board for falls, blocks, 
loose gear, davits, winches, release gear hooks, lugs etc. to confirm compliance 
with proof load requirements and identification of correct and adequate gear. 
Having been satisfied by these preliminary inspections and checks that a test can 
go ahead, a shore or floating crane with an SWL rating of at least 2.2 times the 
fully loaded boat weight (to absorb shock loads in emergency) is to be arranged 
for assisting in the test with safety. 
10.39.9.7 The test is to be carried out by accredited service personnel with a ship’s officer in 
charge (OIC) and witnessed by an authorised person. The OIC is in charge of the 
test at all times and should brief those carrying out the test on what is required. 
The authorised person should take no part in the test and should not be the OIC.

Surveyor appointed by MCA, or other persons authorised by MCA to witness such 
tests. If the authorised person is not an MCA surveyor, then the individual

Maritime Technology Cooperation Centre Caribbean (MTCC Caribbean)

MTCC Caribbean’s Technology Needs Assessment 
1 Summary 
Recognizing that the maritime transport sector is responsible for a sizeable contribution to global 
CO2 emissions, strides have been made toward reducing such emissions from vessels, in addition 
to pursuing reductions in other harmful greenhouse gas emissions. These developments include 
international legal instruments as well as advancements in E nergy Efficient (EE) and Emission 
Abatement T echnologies and methods. However, gaps do exist in the wake of these 
developments as the uptake of new technologies, in particular, is not uniform globally.  
This Technology Needs Assessment (TNA)  focuses on the technological aspect of these 
developments in the context of the Caribbean.  Five categories of stakeholders within the 
Caribbean maritime cluster were identified and targeted for this  assessment, namely; maritime 
administratio
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
developments in the context of the Caribbean.  Five categories of stakeholders within the 
Caribbean maritime cluster were identified and targeted for this  assessment, namely; maritime 
administrations, owners/operators, shipyards/dockyards, technology providers, and ports. A 
couple of the maritime administrations indicated that a technology needs assessment has already 
been carried out in their country, but the majority indicated that none has  been undertaken thus 
far. Survey instruments were drafted and disseminated to the stakeholders and the results 
analyzed to determine the technology needs for the Caribbean region.  
The results of the analysis indicated both the demand and supply for  existing EE and emission 
abatement technologies within the Caribbean region, with disparities being identified between 
owners’ and operators’ awareness of what is available, and what is actually available.  Demand 
for EE and emission abatement technology is affected by the level of awarene
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
s being identified between 
owners’ and operators’ awareness of what is available, and what is actually available.  Demand 
for EE and emission abatement technology is affected by the level of awareness of those 
technologies, and the awareness level of all stakeholders was determined, with owners/operators 
being the most aware. On the supply side, stakeholders identified gaps of varying magnitudes  
between technology available within the Caribbean and internationally available technologies , 
indicating that the supply within the region lags behind what is globally available. 
Several factors affect the decisions of stakeholders with respect to their technological needs and 
selection of appropriate technology. The stakeholders, using a predetermined list of technology 
by MTCC Caribbean, ranked the factors that affect their decision making process. It was 
determined that the most important factors are financial viability and regulatory compliance.  
They also identified the barrie
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
n, ranked the factors that affect their decision making process. It was 
determined that the most important factors are financial viability and regulatory compliance.  
They also identified the barriers that impact the implementation of maritime technology transfer. 
The level of impact of each barrier was rated to determine the greatest challenges faced by the 
region regarding the uptake of EE and emission abatement technology. The largest barriers were 
determined to be high investment costs, lack of finance and the fact that in some instances there 
are no regulatory requirements. 
The assessment determined that in order to overcome these barriers, an enabling environment 
has to be created which will include a robust and comprehensiv e regulatory framework , 
improvements in policy, the removal of organizational and market barriers, and the provision of 
funding mechanisms, among others. To facilitate the creation of an enabling  environment, a 
technology action plan was develope
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
he removal of organizational and market barriers, and the provision of 
funding mechanisms, among others. To facilitate the creation of an enabling  environment, a 
technology action plan was developed which included proposed solutions to each of the identified 
barriers; as means of facilitating the uptake of technology in the region.

MTCC Caribbean’s Technology Needs Assessment 
2 Overview  
Maritime transport emits around 1000 million tonnes of CO2 annually and is responsible for about 
2.5% of global Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions (3rd International Maritime Organization (IMO) 
GHG study). Shipping emissions are predicted to increase between 50% and 250% by 2050 –  
depending on future economic and energy developments.  Ships' energy consumption and CO 2 
emissions could be reduced by up to 75% by applying operational measures and implementing 
existing technologies (2nd IMO GHG study). 
In July 2011, the IM
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
pments.  Ships' energy consumption and CO 2 
emissions could be reduced by up to 75% by applying operational measures and implementing 
existing technologies (2nd IMO GHG study). 
In July 2011, the IMO adopted mandatory measures to improve the EE of international shipping 
through resolution MEPC.203(62) . This was the first legally binding instrument to be adopted 
since the Kyoto Protocol that addresses GHG emissions and the first global mandatory GHG -
reduction regime for an international industry sector. 
All ships of 400 GT and above,  engaged in international trade,  are required to implement and 
maintain a Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) that establishes a mechanism for 
operators to improve the energy efficiency of ships. This should be achieved by monitoring the 
energy efficiency performance of a ship's transportation work, using, for example, the Energy 
Efficiency Operational Indicator (EEOI) as a monitoring and/or benchmarking tool and, at regular 
interva
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
energy efficiency performance of a ship's transportation work, using, for example, the Energy 
Efficiency Operational Indicator (EEOI) as a monitoring and/or benchmarking tool and, at regular 
intervals, considering new technologies and practices to improve energy efficiency. 
The IMO’s MEPC adopted the Initial IMO GHG Strategy in April 2018 (MEPC 72) which marked 
another significant milestone in addressing maritime shipping emissions.  The initial strategy 
identifies levels of ambi tion for the international shipping sector noting that technological 
innovation and the global introduction of alternative fuels and/or energy sources for international 
shipping will be integral to achiev ing the overall ambition. Under the short term measures , the 
initial strategy includes measures to support innovative technologies to further enhance the 
energy efficiency of ships and incentives for first adopters  to develop and take up new 
technologies. It is recognizing that technological devel
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
pport innovative technologies to further enhance the 
energy efficiency of ships and incentives for first adopters  to develop and take up new 
technologies. It is recognizing that technological developments would enable significant 
improvements of the current standards and reduce the harmful impact that ships' exhaust gases 
may have on the environment, ecosystems and human health. 
The strategy also identifies the special needs that LDCs and SIDS have in particular with regard 
to capacity building and technical cooperation. Along with assisting in the efforts to promote low-
carbon technologies by facilitating public-private partnerships and information exchange, the IMO 
continues to provide mechanisms f or facilitating information sharing, technology transfer, 
capacity-building and technical cooperation, taking into account resolution MEPC.229(65) on the 
Promotion of technical co- operation and transfer of technology relating to the improvement of 
energy efficiency of ships.
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
technical cooperation, taking into account resolution MEPC.229(65) on the 
Promotion of technical co- operation and transfer of technology relating to the improvement of 
energy efficiency of ships. 
Many of these measures are cost -effective and offer net benefits, as reduced fuel costs ensure 
the pay-back of any operational or investment costs. Further reductions could be achieved by 
implementing new innovative technologies. 
The viability of many technological options for reducing emissions from ships is becoming better 
established as a result of a range of initiatives at international and national levels. Nevertheless, 
there is a need to find ways by which developing countries can formalize the important process 
of assessing the emerging technologies and practices for adapting to climate change and 
mitigating greenhouse gas emissions from Maritime sector. 
Realizing the decarbonisation targets of the sectors is dependent on the adopt ion of emissions 
control and abatement te
---CHUNK---

climate change and 
mitigating greenhouse gas emissions from Maritime sector. 
Realizing the decarbonisation targets of the sectors is dependent on the adopt ion of emissions 
control and abatement technologies and measures. However, continuous and widespread 
deployment of negative emissions technologies is currently not happening at the required scale.

3 Key Technologies 
The maritime industry has pursued a number of technical and operational measures for reducing 
GHG Emissions from ships at sea and at berth. Technical measures include Emissions Control 
and Energy Efficiency Measures (ECEEMs) ; and operational measures include economies of 
scale, improved voyage planning and the use of alternative fuels.  
The possible emission and energy consumption reduction measures therefore can be achieved 
by using various technical and operational measures called Energy Saving Potentials (ESPs). 
These ESPs can be broadly divided into three categories; 
- Hull resistance reduction, 
- Propulsion efficiency improvement, and 
- Reduction in energy demand. 
For emission reduction, technologica
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
. 
These ESPs can be broadly divided into three categories; 
- Hull resistance reduction, 
- Propulsion efficiency improvement, and 
- Reduction in energy demand. 
For emission reduction, technological measures can further be divided into two major categories;  
- Alternative fuels, and 
- Renewable sources (Alternative sources of energy) 
Bouman et al., 2017 reviewed approximately 150 studies to determine the CO2 reducing potential 
of some key technologies available to the industry. The high degree of uncertainty in CO2 emission 
reduction potential for various ECEEMs was highlighted in these studies. The reason for this 
uncertainty was due to specific  type of vessels and different model assumptions  used in these 
studies. Table 1 provides a summary of the findings.

3.1 Resistance Reduction Methodologies 
The effect of water resistance on the movement of vessels is associated with energy loss, and is 
a major factor in fuel consumption. The total resistance can be divided into;  resistance due to 
viscous; wave making & wave breaking; air resistanc
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
of vessels is associated with energy loss, and is 
a major factor in fuel consumption. The total resistance can be divided into;  resistance due to 
viscous; wave making & wave breaking; air resistance; and appendage resistance. In the design 
phase “length to beam ratio” and beam to draft ratio along with other dimensions also affect ship 
resistance. The selection of optimal dimensions i.e. global optimization, also reduces resistance. 
3.1.1 Frictional Resistance Reduction 
Speed reduction – The ship resistance increases non-linearly with increase in speed. Therefore, 
any reduction in speed leads to reduction in resistance. 
Paints – The advancement s in paint technology has extended the role of hull coating from 
reducing fouling to reducing frictional drag. Hull condition and coating is vital as a 1% increase in 
power is required to maintain speed for a 10 micro millimeter increase in hull roughness. 
Air Lubrication – In this viscous resistance reduction measure, an underwater
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
is vital as a 1% increase in 
power is required to maintain speed for a 10 micro millimeter increase in hull roughness. 
Air Lubrication – In this viscous resistance reduction measure, an underwater air surface is 
provided. The three basic air lubrication methods are: 
- Air cavity – Underwater hull is arranged in a way to allow recirculation of air. Such air 
pockets reduce the viscous resistance by reducing the contact between hull and water. 
- Micro Bubbles – Small bubbles pumped into the underwater hull surface close to the 
boundary layer of the ship. 
- Air Film – Use of special paints to attract air to the hull surface as a film, however the film 
formation is influenced by the water flow speed across the hull.

3.1.2 Hull Form and Appendage optimization. 
Bulbous bow – The use of a Bulbous bow creates a wave interaction which results in reduc ed 
wave resistance. The benefit of a bulbous bow increases with an increase in speed. It is also 
more effective on the full load condition compared to draught in higher conditions.

---CHUNK---

ults in reduc ed 
wave resistance. The benefit of a bulbous bow increases with an increase in speed. It is also 
more effective on the full load condition compared to draught in higher conditions. 
Stern form – Resistance reduction up to 5% is possible by stern modifications. 
Bilge keel  – The bilge keel provides additional longitudinal strength with roll - stability 
improvement. Ideally it should not add to the resistance and therefore requires advanced 
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) optimizations.  
3.1.3 Superstructure optimization 
Minimizing the superstructure with minimal drag shapes reduces air resistance. Air resistance is 
directly dependent on the transverse cross sectional area of a vessel above the water line. The 
appendage modifications not only affect resistance but also the propulsion efficiency. 
3.2 Propeller Design and Efficiency 
Propeller efficiency is defined by the propeller geometry. Propeller efficiency is highly affected by 
cavitation. However, changes
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
lso the propulsion efficiency. 
3.2 Propeller Design and Efficiency 
Propeller efficiency is defined by the propeller geometry. Propeller efficiency is highly affected by 
cavitation. However, changes in blade ratio, geometry, skewness and blade section prevent or 
delay cavitation. A number of active and passive devices in addition to hull form improve wake 
fraction, thrust, rotative and open water efficiency. 
Stern hull – form and positioning of the propeller. 
Wake improvement and Separation Avoidance Devices – These devices optimize wake to 
propeller disk. Examples  include Grothues spoilers, Schneekluth ducts and Mevis duct stern 
tunnels. 
Pre-swirl devices – fins and stators placed in front of the propeller to generate rotational flow in 
front of the propeller. Stator duct combination is usually recommended on bulk carriers. 
Post-swirl devices – These devices convert rotational flow to axial flow and hence placed behind 
the propeller. This also improves rudder performance,
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
nation is usually recommended on bulk carriers. 
Post-swirl devices – These devices convert rotational flow to axial flow and hence placed behind 
the propeller. This also improves rudder performance, for example - boss cap fin. 
3.3 Reduction in energy demand 
Shaft generator – Shaft generator can be utilized if controllable pitch propeller is used. Fixed 
pitch propeller shafts can also be used but only during sea voyages. Shaft generator increases 
the power demand on main engine but saves on the fuel consu mption for electrical power 
generator. 
Waste heat Recovery – the exhaust gas from the main engine can be used to generate steam. 
The surplus heat is utilized to drive the exhaust gas turbine or to fulfil the other requirements on 
the ship. The heat recover y can be made through conventional heat exchangers from cooling 
water and recovery from exhaust gas boiler (EGB). However, this is only available when the main 
engine is running.

water and recovery from exhaust gas boiler (EGB). However, this is only available when the main 
engine is running.

Weight optimization – The displacement of the vessel not only increases resis tance but also 
demands higher propulsion power. Weight savings can be achieved using a variety of measures. 
For example, the use of high tensile steel can offer up to 2% reduction in fuel consumption. 
Efficient Lighting system – Installing a low energy consumption system will reduce the power 
requirements of auxiliary engines on-board. It will also reduce the energy demands for the lighting 
of the ship. 
Use of Renewable Energy – Kite sailing; very large free flying sails, supplement the propulsion 
generated by the engines and reduce fuel consumption by using wind power. The system consists 
of a kite, an automotive control system

sailing; very large free flying sails, supplement the propulsion 
generated by the engines and reduce fuel consumption by using wind power. The system consists 
of a kite, an automotive control system and a launch & recovery system.

In addition to measures being implemented by ships, major ports around the world have already 
begun implementing programmes and policies to address emissions from ships while in or arriving 
at port. These programmes are a mix of operational, technical, regulatory and incentive measures. 
On the technical and operational front,
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
olicies to address emissions from ships while in or arriving 
at port. These programmes are a mix of operational, technical, regulatory and incentive measures. 
On the technical and operational front, measures such as cold ironing and just in time arrival are 
being supported and encouraged. Port incentive programmes that favour and attract ships with 
modern and GHG efficient designs  could have some effect (Winnes et al., 2015). However, 
greater impacts are more likely to result from international regulations than f rom individual port 
programmes. 
Single measures or incentives will not provide significant reductions in GHG emissions bu t a 
combination of a number of them have proven to be most beneficial. According to the IMO, it has 
been estimated that through ESPs, ships’ energy consumption and emissions can be reduced by 
as much as 75% by implementing existing technologies and proven operational measures. 
However applying these solutions with such high degrees of performanc
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
onsumption and emissions can be reduced by 
as much as 75% by implementing existing technologies and proven operational measures. 
However applying these solutions with such high degrees of performance uncertainties and costly 
investments has resulted in sluggish industry action; this TNA aims to, among others, determine 
the technology needs of the region to improve the sluggishness of industry response.

4 Methodology 
Available research and literature in shipping indicate that it is possible to improve energy 
efficiency and reduce emissions in a cost -effective manner using technology (Lindstad et al., 
2015a; Buhaug et al., 2009; Faber et al., 2009, 2011; Alvik et al., 2010).  However, these studies 
are limited in scope as they address  mainly CO2 reduction potential at the m acro level and/or 
investigation of individual or combined technol
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
09, 2011; Alvik et al., 2010).  However, these studies 
are limited in scope as they address  mainly CO2 reduction potential at the m acro level and/or 
investigation of individual or combined technological and operational m easures reducing 
emissions. 
There is an abundance of studies presenting mitigation measures and scenarios for shipping but 
comprehensive reviews on this issue are limited in scientific literature. To quantify the maximum 
potential for GHG reduction and ene rgy efficiency measures is complex due to various 
organizational, technical, economic and political barriers for implementation. The application of 
these measures is also dependent on distinct ship types and age. Therefore, it is essential to take 
into account the viewpoint of each stakeholder. This TNA attempts to capture the viewpoint of 
stakeholders within the Caribbean Region. In this regard, objectives of this technology needs 
assessment carried out by MTCC Caribbean are to: 
1. Determine the availa
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
ts to capture the viewpoint of 
stakeholders within the Caribbean Region. In this regard, objectives of this technology needs 
assessment carried out by MTCC Caribbean are to: 
1. Determine the available technologies in the participating countries; 
2. Determine the technology gaps that exist; 
3. Determine the technology needs of participating countries; 
4. Determine the barriers to implementing their technology needs; and 
5. Determine the actions required to help overcome these barriers.

 Key Stakeholders  
Key stakeholders were identified and grouped according to the following categories: 
 
1. Maritime Administrations – These are responsible for regulation and enforcement in 
their capacities as Flag Sta
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
y stakeholders were identified and grouped according to the following categories: 
 
1. Maritime Administrations – These are responsible for regulation and enforcement in 
their capacities as Flag State Administrations and Port State Control (PSC), which makes 
them one of the major drivers of technology uptake in the region. Maritime administrations 
are also the main focal points between the IMO and the local maritime industry, ensuring 
compliance with international maritime instruments via enforce ment through national 
instruments. As the primary government entity responsible for regulating shipping, 
maritime administrations can implement incentive program mes that will encourage 
vessels calling within their jurisdiction to uptake EE and emission abatement technology, 
cleaner marine fuels, and other methods that achieve reductions in harmful GHG 
emissions while at port. MTCC Caribbean sought the knowledge and expertise of the 
maritime administrations of the 16 Caribbean terri
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
e fuels, and other methods that achieve reductions in harmful GHG 
emissions while at port. MTCC Caribbean sought the knowledge and expertise of the 
maritime administrations of the 16 Caribbean territories under its ambit to determine the 
needs of the region from the standpoint of the regulators. Refer to appendix I for the list of 
maritime administrations that provided responses for the technology needs assessment. 
 
2. Vessel Owners/Operators – These are the principle users of EE and emission abatement 
technology. As the end users and those chiefly affected by changes in technology 
requirements, technology design must balance their needs while meeting international 
regulatory requirements; making the needs of vessel owners/ operators of paramount 
importance. There have been mixed responses by owners/operators regarding the current 
and impending 2020 fuel Sulphur content cap. The demand by ship owners/operators for 
particular technologies is impacted by the availability of t
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
responses by owners/operators regarding the current 
and impending 2020 fuel Sulphur content cap. The demand by ship owners/operators for 
particular technologies is impacted by the availability of that technology; making the 
determination of their demand of critical importance for the suppliers in the region. They 
will also be able to identify the barriers and challenges that need to be addressed to 
achieve compliance with upcoming regulatory requirements. R efer to appendix II for the 
list of vessel owners/operators that provided responses for the TNA. 
 
3. Shipyards and Dockyards – These are the facilitators of green technology uptake. They 
function as the bridge between technology providers and vessel owners/ operators. 
Shipyards and Dockyards are uniquely positioned to be highly familiar with a wide range 
of technologies and ship types, and may possess an enhanced understanding of the 
needs of all parties involved. Their importance as a respondent lies with their ability
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
ly familiar with a wide range 
of technologies and ship types, and may possess an enhanced understanding of the 
needs of all parties involved. Their importance as a respondent lies with their ability to 
provide the supply of and facilitate installation/retrofitting of EE and emission abatement 
technology.  MTCC Caribbean was unable to secure a response from a 
shipyard/dockyard. Refer to appendix III for a letter from Caribbean Dockyard and 
Engineering Services Limited (Caridoc) explaining why they believe the survey was not 
applicable to them.

used and regulated by other stakeholders in the maritime cluster. The technology uptake

6 Enabling Environment 
Maritime technology developers  are not based in the Caribbean. The m ajority of technology 
transfer is facilitated on a case by case basis between ship owners/operators and the technology 
providers.  Although technology transfer is oft en a private interaction between two companies, 
institutional barriers and policies influence the transaction process, as well as the efficiency of the 
transfer process. Under perfect market conditions, all additional needs for energy services would 
be provided by the lowest cost measures, whether energy supply increases or energy demand 
reduces. There is considerable evidence that substantial energy efficiency investments are not 
made even when they are lower in cost than marginal energy supply . This condi tion therefore 
suggest that market barriers exist and there is therefore a need for policy i
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
ciency investments are not 
made even when they are lower in cost than marginal energy supply . This condi tion therefore 
suggest that market barriers exist and there is therefore a need for policy intervention to create 
an enabling environment.  
The enabling environment for technology transfer in the maritime sector involves a complex 
interface of human factor, institutional knowledge, institutional capacity and ships (type and age). 
In the case of low carbon technologies, especially maritime technologies, there are elements of 
both vertical and horizontal transfer, as illustrated in the figure 8 below, especially given the need 
for commercialization within the  regional context. It is also imperative to state here that 
commercial acceptance within the maritime sector is influenced by logical business sense and 
mandatory requirements and compliance within the operating region. For technology transfer to 
be effective, the targeted receivers must be able to adopt, implement an
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
d by logical business sense and 
mandatory requirements and compliance within the operating region. For technology transfer to 
be effective, the targeted receivers must be able to adopt, implement and sustain the technology. 
Adoption, implementation and sustainability of technology are linked to each other  and the 
absence of any single component can lead to the failure of the maritime technology transfer 
process. The uncertainties of the maritime sector demand a more supporting environment when 
compared to other sectors.  
Figure 8 - Avenues for technology transfer 
 
To create a win -win scenario for technology adapters and providers, the creation of a genuine 
collaborative environment is required. C reating an enabling environment  at each stage of the

value chain must be considered (Singh and Rambarath-Parasram, 2018) (Rambarath-Parasram, 
et al., 2018). It is not only important to lift the existing constraints but also to fill the gaps which 
exist in existing regulatory and administrative mechanisms. This situation may be resolved given 
the var ious initiatives specific to the maritime sector that have been brought by the IMO. In 
MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 23, emphasis is laid on co- operation along with transfer by 
promoting technical cooperation towards efficiency of ships. The ena
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
tor that have been brought by the IMO. In 
MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 23, emphasis is laid on co- operation along with transfer by 
promoting technical cooperation towards efficiency of ships. The enabling environment requires 
the following four components: 
• Relevant Policy; 
• Relevant Statutes; 
• Institutional R esponsibility for developing rules and  implementing programmes, 
(which in some instances may involve developing existing and new institutional 
capacities), and 
• Funding Mechanisms for capacity building and technology uptake. 
Any successful policy reform supporting an enabling environment requires changes in 
implementation that facilitates compliance for targeted stakeholders. Such intervention will need 
to be cognizant of the incentives that drive business decisions. The development of the maritime 
sector is on the legislative agenda of many Caribbean territories. However, current top down 
approaches have failed to achieve desired results in the absence of suppo
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
The development of the maritime 
sector is on the legislative agenda of many Caribbean territories. However, current top down 
approaches have failed to achieve desired results in the absence of support from the bottom level. 
The enabling environment therefore, should address the disparity between the available 
technologies and the technology in use , and will facilitate co -operation among regional 
administrations. Such cooperation should be directed toward the removal of barriers and adopt a 
framework which is efficient for receiving the required technology. This will require investment into 
institutions, infrastructure and the socio- economic environment. Capacity building is required to 
extract and absorb the complete benefits of the new technology adapted.  Institutional capacities 
will need to be prepared accordingly. 
While financial considerations and regulatory compliance are noted drivers for energy efficiency, 
the inadequacy of the enforcement of international standa
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
ies 
will need to be prepared accordingly. 
While financial considerations and regulatory compliance are noted drivers for energy efficiency, 
the inadequacy of the enforcement of international standards in the region creates an environment 
where ship operators do not perceive the need to comply. Gov ernment intervention is likely to 
play a key role in facilitating low carbon technology transfer by developing a suitable policy. The 
business case for the uptake of energy efficiency can only be made when operating costs are 
reduced or capital costs reduced when compared to existing operational conditions. Most existing 
policies and programmes for  the transfer of environmentally sound and greenhouse gas 
abatement technologies are addressed to national needs and rarely address the needs of the 
maritime sector, as it is not adequately included in many Caribbean NDCs.  
Therefore to overcome the aforementioned challenges, future research is required to address the 
following: 
• Comp
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
of the 
maritime sector, as it is not adequately included in many Caribbean NDCs.  
Therefore to overcome the aforementioned challenges, future research is required to address the 
following: 
• Complexity of the sector and address the interlinked nature of such factor s (human 
and institutional); 
• Absorption and Adaption of technology including investment into capacity building; 
• Policy influence and institutional drivers, as major components of technology transfer; 
• Organizational and Market barriers  which affect the process of technology transfer; 
and 
• Policy and Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) regime.

7 Technology Action Plan 
The Technology Action Plan (TAP) is a plan for the uptake and diffusion of technologies based 
on identified priorities that will contribute to maritime climate change mitigation and adaptation. 
Therefore, this TAP is made
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
an (TAP) is a plan for the uptake and diffusion of technologies based 
on identified priorities that will contribute to maritime climate change mitigation and adaptation. 
Therefore, this TAP is made up of numerous specific actions. The TAP is not technology-specific, 
but covers a portfolio of technologies as assessed under the  Technology Needs Assessment  
(TNA). The same set of Actions will benefit all technologies. 
The Technology Action Plan is the final outcome of the TNA. This plan outl ines pathways for 
implementation of technology transfer based on the feedback received in the TNA. The TAP 
captures the: 
- Identification and description of required actions for implementing Technology Transfer 
- Identification of activities needed to implement identified actions 
- Stakeholder engagement for these activities

MTCC Caribbean’s Technology Needs Assessment 
 Planning and Management 
The activities and stakeholder engagement for each measure will require the necessary 
resources, including costs and the funding needs for the specific Actions and Activities . 
Considering budget constraints , further consultation with stakeholders within the region is 
necessary. These activities can be grouped into two categories encompassing a Regional 
Approach in the Diffusion of EE Technologies and the Implementation of Specific Prioritized 
Technology. 
7.2.1 A Regional Approach in the Diffusion of EE Technologies 
A
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
ies encompassing a Regional 
Approach in the Diffusion of EE Technologies and the Implementation of Specific Prioritized 
Technology. 
7.2.1 A Regional Approach in the Diffusion of EE Technologies 
A Regional Approach with the establishment of a programme covering all interrelated actions for 
the diffusion of EE technologies. These activities will require large scale funding and depend on 
international donors or public sector grants . These activities can be covered under capacity 
building initiatives at regional levels. 
7.2.2 Implementation of Specific Prioritized Technology 
The implementation of s pecific prioritized technology is  expected to be sponsored by the 
stakeholders benefitting from such activity. Activities and Small scale technology uptake pilot 
projects are expected to provide solutions to the issues arising from this TNA. 
7.2.3 Next Phase 
The activities in the next phase must be aligned with the top priorities identified by stakeholders 
in this TNA, namely: 
-
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
o provide solutions to the issues arising from this TNA. 
7.2.3 Next Phase 
The activities in the next phase must be aligned with the top priorities identified by stakeholders 
in this TNA, namely: 
- Economics of Maritime Operations after the uptake of EE Technology 
- Availability of Financial Support for uptake of EE technology 
- Upcoming Regulations/Future Legal Requirements 
Based on the stakeholder feedback, t he awareness of the need for interventions to facilitate 
reduced emissions and the GHG reduction potential of EE technologies seems to be sufficiently 
covered by various past capacity building activities. It may be useful to explore the feasibility of 
focussed capacity building in one regional shipyard in EE technology transfer to facilitate a one 
stop shop for end user s. This can be achieved through a pilot project in  the next phase of the 
project.

first phase will

project.

first phase will further refine the TAP activities.

MTCC Caribbean’s Technology Needs Assessment 
8 Limitations 
MTCC Caribbean encountered several challenges during the undertaking of the technology needs 
assessment which are as follows; 
1. Low response rate to the surveys – Of the seventy three (73) targeted stakeholders, only 
thirty (30) responses were received.  
 
2. Incomplete survey submissions – Some respondents did not answer all  questions. One 
respondent explained that he did not have sufficient/accurate information to complete the 
survey due to the lack of cooperation within different government agencies in his country 
(Antigua & Barbuda). 
 
3. Misinterpretation of the questions – Particular sections of the sur
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: MTCC-Caribbeans-National-Technology-Needs-and-Barriers-Report-for-publication.pdf
complete the 
survey due to the lack of cooperation within different government agencies in his country 
(Antigua & Barbuda). 
 
3. Misinterpretation of the questions – Particular sections of the survey may have been 
confusing for some of the respondents, and they may have misinterpreted the priority 
ranking questions, which affected the results. 
 
4. Communication of survey – The survey was conducted online, and as such a survey link 
was forwarded to participants to complete. There were instances where the ema il 
addresses used were no longer operational or email accounts were too full and links were 
not delivered. Additionally, challenges were also encountered concerning attempts to 
follow up using newly obtained operational email addresses and phone calls to 
stakeholders to request responses.

10.11.1.1 Past Technology Needs Assessments 
The ten (10) respondents indicated whether a technology needs assessment has been conducted 
within their country with respect to Energy Efficiency and Emissions Abatement methods, which 
is illustrated in figure 10 below. 
Figure 10 - Past Technology Needs Assessments 
 
Eight (8) of the ten (10) respondents indicated that no technology needs assessment  regarding 
Energy Efficiency and Emissions Abatement methods  has been conducted within their country, 
while two (2) respondents indicated that an analysis has been conducted. (St. Kitts and Belize)

Maritime Profile of India
4
• India’s Vast Maritime Network:
• India has one of the world’s largest Exclusive Economic Zones 
(EEZ) covering 2.37 million sq. km.
• 13 major ports and around 200 smaller ports contribute 
significantly to global trade, with heavy vessel traffic in critical 
zones such as Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata.
• Major shipping lanes, anchorage areas, and fairways include the 
Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, and the Indian Ocean—all crucial for 
international shipping routes.

Maritime Profile of India
6
India’s Exclusive Economic Zone
India has the 18th largest Exclusive Economic Zone globally with a total area of more 
than 2 million sq km. In the southwestern coast of India lies the Lakshadweep group 
island in the Laccadive Sea, and the Andaman and Nicobar lie in the Bay of Bengal 
and the Andaman Sea. In the west, India’s EEZ is bordered by Pakistan, in the south 
by the Maldives and Sri Lanka, and in the east by Bangladesh, Malaysia, Myanmar, 
Indonesia and Thailand.
India has a greater benefit as it has a coastline stretch of 7,500 km and India’s 
exclusive control over the EEZ resources is the navigation of seafaring trade and 
transport vessels in the zone.

Current URN Scenario in India

Policy and Regulatory Framework
Existing Legislation:
• Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification: Primarily aimed at managing 
India's coastal  areas, but the regulations could  be adapted to include 
noise pollution.
• Environmental Protection Act: Cove
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: Mahesh Korade and Dr Ashokan IMO WMU WORKSHOP India.pdf
Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification: Primarily aimed at managing 
India's coastal  areas, but the regulations could  be adapted to include 
noise pollution.
• Environmental Protection Act: Covers pollution controls, with opportunities 
to expand into  marine noise regulation.
• India has various laws for the protection of marine biodiversity, including the 
Wildlife Protection Act (WPA) of 1972 and the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) 
Notification (2011/2019). These provide indirect protection against noise pollution 
by safeguarding habitats of marine species like dolphins and sea turtles.
• However, no specific legislation exists for URN in India currently. This represents a 
significant regulatory gap, which is being evaluated.

Previous, Ongoing, and Future Initiatives
14
• Assessment of URN:
Pilot projects have been conducted in collaboration with institutions like the Ministry of 
Earth Sciences (MoES) and National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) to assess underwater n
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: Mahesh Korade and Dr Ashokan IMO WMU WORKSHOP India.pdf
Assessment of URN:
Pilot projects have been conducted in collaboration with institutions like the Ministry of 
Earth Sciences (MoES) and National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) to assess underwater noise 
in Indian waters.
Installation of hydrophones in select areas to monitor the noise levels from shipping 
activities, particularly around Mumbai port, is part of an ongoing initiative.
Technical Infrastructure:
India is in the process of building a network of URN monitoring stations along major 
shipping lanes, using hydrophones to track noise levels and establish baseline data.
Collaborations with international bodies, including the IMO’s GloNoise Partnership and the 
International Whaling Commission (IWC), have enhanced India’s technical capacity to assess URN 
impacts.

Previous, Ongoing, and Future Initiatives
15
1.Port Efficiency Programs:
India has launched programs like ‘Just in Time Arrivals’ at some major ports, including Mumbai and Cochin, 
reducing ship idling times and t
---CHUNK---

oing, and Future Initiatives
15
1.Port Efficiency Programs:
India has launched programs like ‘Just in Time Arrivals’ at some major ports, including Mumbai and Cochin, 
reducing ship idling times and thus lowering noise generation.
India is exploring ways to enhance vessel traffic management systems to minimize noise pollution in critical 
zones.
2. Renewable Energy Integration:
The growing adoption of wind and wave energy along India's coasts also creates opportunities to integrate 
noise reduction strategies in energy-related marine activities.
3. Future Plans:
India is planning to initiate more comprehensive studies on URN impacts, especially around Marine Protected 
Areas (MPAs), to fine-tune mitigation strategies.
The government is in talks with IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 project to explore more fuel-efficient, noise-reducing 
technologies for India’s expanding fleet.

Previous, Ongoing, and Future Initiatives
16
Legal Framework:
India's Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 (WLPA) provides legal protection to 
marine mammals along the Indian coastline. 
Shore Power Implementation:
All Indian ports are committed to supplying shore power to ships whenever 
possible, reducing the need for ships to run their engines while docked. 
The Directorate General of Shipping (DGS) has issued Standard Operating 
Procedures (SOPs) for the implementation of shore power supply in Indian 
ports.

and create an environmentally friendly ecosystem at all major ports. 
Target: 60% green power by 2030 and 100% green power by 2050.

• Propeller modifications and innovative hull designs can reduce URN. India is 
exploring quieter engines and operational changes (e.g., reducing vessel speed) 
to minimize noise impacts.

reefs and marine parks.
Acoustic Monitoring Systems:

Stakeholders and Collaborative Efforts
Government Agencies:
MoES and MoEFCC are key players in policy and research. 
MoES funds marine research institutes,  while MoEFCC 
regulates environmental  impacts
Private Sector: 
Indian shipbuilders and the shipping industry are investing

have initiated design modifications aimed at reducing URN.

NGOs like Wildlife Trust of India and international 
collaborators like WWF are working on awareness and 
advocacy for quieter seas.

Challenges and Future Prospects
20
Challenges:
Data Limitations: 
There is limited real-time data on URN impacts 
in India. Most research is in the early stages.
Costs: 
Implementing noise-reduction technologies in older 
ships can be expensive
.Lack of Awareness:
Many in the maritime industry are still unaware of

Research Expansion: 
Increased funding and research into URN’s 
impact on Indian marine life.

University can help transfer noise-
reduction technologies to India.
Indian National Task Force: 
This body, formed as part of the GloNoise 
project, is tasked with integrating international 
guidelines into India’s maritime practices.

Brief:
• MoES has been focusing on development of acoustic systems for
Passive Acoustic Monitoring in the shallow and deep ocean and further
analysis along with ancillary data such as CTD, wind/ wave/ rainfall,
and sediment for acoustical oceanographic applications, underwater
communication and coastal surveillance.

system (ANMS) and operated successfully at many coastal regions of
India.
• Acoustical oceanographic, anthropogenic, geo-acoustics and bio-
acoustic applications have been studied in detail from time series data
obtained from the system including during extreme events such as
cyclones.
• The underwater Acoustic Test Facility in NIOT is the only accredited
facility in India which caters to testing and calibration underwater
acoustic sensors.

Manning Agency Guidelines
5
Introduction
These guidelines have been produced to help shipping companies choose reputable manning agencies and 
to ensure that seafarers are recruited in line with the requirements of the ILO Maritime Labour Convention 
2006 (MLC, 2006). 
The guidelines aim to:
• Provide clear advice to companies on what to consider when i
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: Manning-Agency-Guidelines (1).pdf
at seafarers are recruited in line with the requirements of the ILO Maritime Labour Convention 
2006 (MLC, 2006). 
The guidelines aim to:
• Provide clear advice to companies on what to consider when identifying a manning agency;
• Advise shipping or ship management companies which have their own internal or ‘owned’ manning 
agencies, on how to operate them in line with legal requirements and best practice;
• Ensure companies know how to audit manning agencies to the IMO International Safety Management 
Code (ISM) and the ILO MLC, 2006 requirements;
• Encourage governments to operate systems to regulate recruitment and placement services for 
seafarers in accordance with MLC, 2006 through licensing or alternative means;
• Advise shipowners what to do when targeted by fraudulent operators that falsely advertise using their 
name;
• Help shipowners ensure their relationship with their manning agencies upholds seafarers’ rights and 
welfare; and
• Strengthen the provisions in the MLC, 2006

• Help shipowners ensure their relationship with their manning agencies upholds seafarers’ rights and 
welfare; and
• Strengthen the provisions in the MLC, 2006. 
What is a Manning Agency?
A manning agency is a company that fulfils the following functions: 
• Advertises a vacancy and gathers applications;
• Proposes seafarers/candidates to principals/clients;
• Arranges medical and visa requirements for outgoing seafarers; 
• Arranges most local procedures/requirements for crew joining; and
• Is generally understood as providing ‘recruitment and placement services’ as referred to in the MLC, 2006.
What is a Crew Manager?
A crew manager is a company that employs seafarers on behalf of a ship manager or shipowner or on its 
own behalf. A crew manager fulfils the functions set out below and operates as follows:
• Signs crew management agreements with shipowners (e.g. Crewman A, Crewman B or similar);
• Interviews seafarers, ensures all licences and

ILO Maritime Labour Convention, 2006
Regulation 1.4 and Standard A1.4 aim to ensure that seafarers can access an efficient and well-regulated 
seafarer recruitment and placement system. It contains requirements for public and private services whose 
primary purpose is the recruitment and placement of seafarers or which recruit and place a significant 
number of seafarers, namely:
• All seafarers shall have access to an efficient, adequate and accountable system for finding employment 
on board ship without charge to the seafarer;
• Shipowners who use seafarer recruitment and placement services that are based in countries or 
territories that are not parties to the MLC, 2006 must ensure that those services conform to MLC, 2006 
requirements;
• Public seafarer recruitment and placement services must be operated in an orderly manner protecting 
and promoting seafarers’ employment rights;
• Private seafarer recruitment a
---CHUNK---
SOURCE: Manning-Agency-Guidelines (1).pdf
2006 
requirements;
• Public seafarer recruitment and placement services must be operated in an orderly manner protecting 
and promoting seafarers’ employment rights;
• Private seafarer recruitment and placement services must comply with a system of licensing or 
certification or other form of regulation; 
• These provisions shall also apply to recruitment and placement services operated by a seafarers’ 
organisation in the member’s territory for the supply of seafarers who are their nationals to ships flying 
their flag; 
• Seafarer recruitment and placement services are prohibited from using means, mechanisms or lists 
intended to prevent or deter seafarers gaining employment they are qualified for;
• No fees or other charges for seafarer recruitment or placement, or for providing employment to seafarers, 
may be borne directly or indirectly, in whole or in part, by seafarers, other than the cost of the seafarer 
obtaining a national statutory medical certificate, the national seafa

• Seafarer recruitment and placement services maintain an up-to-date register of all seafarers recruited or 
placed by them, for the competent authority to be able to inspect.
